justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an asset trading near 259–261 range. For the 1-day estimate of 259.5, I was essentially anchoring close to the last known price, assuming mean-reversion tendencies dominate over very short horizons and that no major catalysts were imminent. The 1-week estimate of 261 incorporates a slight upward drift, consistent with a mild positive momentum assumption or a small risk premium for holding over a week. The 1-month estimate of 265 extends that drift further, reflecting the general tendency of risk assets to trend slightly upward over monthly horizons in the absence of negative shocks, while also acknowledging that more time allows for larger directional moves to accumulate.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the fundamental reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, a 21-point range (249–270) captures typical intraday-to-next-day volatility, including gap risk from overnight news. By one week, the 36-point range (243–279) accounts for the possibility of a meaningful macro announcement, earnings event, or sentiment shift. At one month, the 74-point range (228–302) reflects the full spectrum of scenarios possible over approximately 20 trading days, including trend continuation, reversal, or sideways consolidation punctuated by volatility spikes.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the downside, a sudden macro shock — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, geopolitical escalation, or a disappointing economic data release — could drive prices well below 228 over the monthly horizon. Liquidity crises or forced selling events can produce moves that dwarf normal volatility estimates. On the upside, a strong catalyst such as better-than-expected earnings, a dovish surprise, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above 302.

It is also worth noting that my intervals are constructed around a roughly symmetric assumption of uncertainty, which may not hold in practice. Many financial assets exhibit negative skew, meaning large downside moves tend to be more abrupt and severe than equivalent upside moves. If that asymmetry is present here, the true lower bound of the 90% interval may deserve to be set wider than the upper bound, and users of this forecast should weight tail-risk scenarios on the downside with somewhat more caution than the symmetric intervals might suggest.
